Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis differ on a synagogue without an attendant’s residence.
Another solution distinguishes synagogues with and without a residence.
A third solution starts with both lacking a residence and continues on the next daf.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The proposed distinction puts the exempt synagogue in a city and the liable one in a village.
Are city synagogues really exempt from house leprosy?
A teaching excludes Jerusalem but Rabbi Yehuda excludes only the Temple site, implying that ordinary city buildings can be affected.
This implication includes urban synagogues, contrary to the proposed distinction.
The wording is corrected: Rabbi Yehuda meant only a sacred place is excluded.
What underlying disagreement divides the teachers?
They disagree whether Jerusalem was apportioned to individual tribes.
A teaching allocates parts of the Temple precinct to Judah and Benjamin.
It describes a strip of Judah under the altar and Benjamin’s longing to absorb it.
Scriptural language about Benjamin supports the claim that the divine presence rested in his territory.
A contrary teacher holds that Jerusalem was never apportioned to the tribes.
The rule against renting Jerusalem houses and beds shows that residents had no exclusive ownership there.
Abaye derives the etiquette of leaving a bottle and skin for one’s host.
Can village synagogues become impure through house leprosy?
A teaching requires a conquered and apportioned holding clearly assigned to its owner.
“The one whose house it is” excludes property not individually designated to a person.
The earlier solutions to the synagogue contradiction remain the sound explanation.
The mishna requires a replacement priest to be prepared.
A replacement can be initiated through the morning offering if the disqualification occurs beforehand.
How is he initiated if the High Priest becomes unfit after that offering?
Rav Adda proposes initiating him through the distinctive belt.
That works if the regular High Priest and ordinary priest wear the same belt.
If their belts differ, the proposal does not explain the initiation.
Abaye proposes wearing all eight garments and turning a burning limb on the altar.
Rav Huna treats turning the limb as sacrificial service, so it can effect initiation.
Rav Pappa begins another answer, continued on the next side.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The replacement priest is initiated through his first act of service.
Is there precedent for service itself conferring sacred status?
Moses’ vessels were anointed, but later vessels were consecrated by use.
The priest’s own service can likewise initiate him.
Rav Dimi reports a dispute over whether the ordinary priest’s belt was wool and linen or plain linen.
A teaching contrasts the High Priest and ordinary priest only by their belts, potentially identifying Rabbi’s position.
If this refers to ordinary days, the priests differ in more than their belts.
The suggested reading therefore places the comparison on Yom Kippur.
The comparison might instead concern only garments both priests share during the year.
Ravin clarifies the agreed materials for the High Priest’s belt on Yom Kippur and other days.
The disagreement concerns the ordinary priest’s belt: Rabbi says mixed fabric, and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says linen.
Rav Nahman introduces a teaching on the priestly garments used to remove altar ashes.
Rabbi Yehuda includes the turban and belt, while Rabbi Dosa allows the High Priest’s Yom Kippur garments for an ordinary priest.
Rabbi rejects Rabbi Dosa because the two priests’ belts are different.
He also objects to using garments of greater sanctity for lesser service.
He interprets the extra wording as permitting worn garments.
A teaching reads the command to leave the Yom Kippur garments as requiring their storage.
Rabbi Dosa reads it only as barring the High Priest from reusing them on another Yom Kippur.
A replacement who served after the original priest became unfit retains the obligations of High Priesthood according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yosei allows the original to return but bars the replacement from serving in either rank.
Rabbi Yosei cites Yosef ben Elem as an instance where the Sages imposed that rule.
Two High Priests risk antagonism, and sacred rank may be raised but not lowered.
Rabba bar bar Hana begins to cite Rabbi Yohanan, continued on the next side.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ruling follows Rabbi Yosei, yet a replacement’s service remains valid if performed.
Rav adds that the replacement resumes service if the original High Priest dies.
Why state what seems obvious?
The ruling dispels concern that rivalry in the first priest’s lifetime bars the replacement later.
Rabbi Yehuda requires preparing a second wife.
Why do the Rabbis prepare a priest but not a wife?
Impurity is common while death is not.
The Rabbis argue that Rabbi Yehuda’s concern would require endlessly many wives.
Rabbi Yehuda worries about one death, not the much rarer death of two wives.
The Rabbis maintain that this reasoning cannot set a firm limit.
Should the Rabbis then demand multiple replacement priests too?
A High Priest is vigilant against impurity.
If so, why prepare even one substitute?
Having a substitute makes him still more careful.
How does merely preparing a woman make her the priest’s “house,” his wife?
He betroths her.
Betrothal without marriage does not yet make her his household.
He marries her.
Then he has two households, though the verse speaks of one.
He divorces the second woman.
Ordinary divorce revives the problem of having no replacement wife.
A conditional divorce tied to her death is proposed.
If she survives, both marriages remain and there are two households.
The opposite condition would divorce her if she survives and leave the original wife if she dies.
If the original wife dies while the second is divorced, he has no wife.
A condition tied to the death of either woman is proposed.
If neither dies, he again has two households.
Can a divorce dependent on such a condition be legally valid?
Rava distinguishes a lifetime condition preventing severance from one tied to a third party’s life.
A divorce conditional on the other wife surviving seems to leave one wife in either outcome.
If the first wife dies during the service, the condition changes its status retroactively; the problem continues next side.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The first wife’s death could retroactively leave him serving while married to two women.
A divorce conditioned on the other wife’s death is tried instead.
If the other wife dies, that condition leaves him without a wife.
He gives both wives conditional divorces, one tied to the other’s survival and one to avoiding the synagogue.
Both conditions could be met and leave him without either wife.
A revised pair of conditions makes the second divorce depend on his own synagogue entry.
If either wife dies, the arrangement can leave the other as his sole wife.
Could a death during service reveal that he had two wives earlier in the day?
He can enter the synagogue before a wife dies, making her divorce retroactively effective.
Rav Asi challenges the singular “house” reasoning by comparison with two widows eligible for levirate marriage.
The repeated “his yevama” includes a man who left two wives.
Ravina similarly challenges exclusion of a betrothed woman from levirate marriage.
The word “outside” includes a betrothed woman in that law.
A baraita allows an acutely mourning High Priest to offer sacrifices, though not eat them; Rabbi Yehuda adds “the whole day.”
What does Rabbi Yehuda mean by “the whole day”?
Rava initially says he is brought from home to serve.
Abaye objects from Rabbi Yehuda’s rule that a priest who hears of a death leaves his service.
Rava withdraws that reading and begins a new interpretation, continued next side.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda bars service for the entire mourning day lest the priest eat consecrated food.
Rav Adda notes that Rabbi Yehuda nonetheless lets a High Priest serve if his wife dies on Yom Kippur.
On a fast day nobody eats; on an ordinary day the mourner could inadvertently eat.
Would acute mourning apply to a wife whom he conditionally divorced?
Even without legal mourning, grief could distract him.
The mishna lists services the High Priest performs during his seven days of preparation.
At other times he may choose to offer and receive the first portion.
Rav Hisda asks how this can fit Rabbi Akiva, who says sprinkling purifies the impure but defiles the pure.
A baraita attributes that view of red-heifer water to Rabbi Akiva.
The Sages read the rule as distinguishing targets susceptible to impurity.
What practical rule follows from their reading?
A mishna distinguishes water sprayed on a person from water sprayed on an animal.
What textual basis supports Rabbi Akiva?
The verse specifies an impure target, which Rabbi Akiva contrasts with a pure target.
The Sages use that phrase for susceptible objects and reason that a pure person remains pure.
Rabbi Akiva invokes Solomon’s admission that this red-heifer rule exceeds ordinary reasoning.
The Sages locate the puzzle in why sprinkling leaves people pure while touching the water defiles.
The verse seems to declare the sprinkler impure; how can he remain pure?
A proposed reading treats “sprinkler” as “one who touches.”
The verse separately names touching and assigns it a different degree of impurity.
The term is instead read as one who carries the water.
Why does the Torah say “sprinkles” if it means “carries”?
The term specifies enough water to perform sprinkling.
What if sprinkling itself has no minimum volume?
The lack of minimum applies to the drops on a person; a vessel still needs enough water.
A mishna begins to define the vessel’s required amount, continued next side.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna requires enough water to immerse the hyssop tips.
Abaye reconciles the prior mishna even with Rabbi Akiva by placing sprinkling after the day’s service.
The mishna’s order seems to put incense before cleaning the lamps.
The order in Tamid lists lamp cleaning before incense.
Rav Huna initially attributes Tamid to Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpa.
An anonymous Tamid rule gives one application of blood at each of two altar corners.
A teaching identifies Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpa as dissenting from that anonymous rule.
Rabbi Yohanan instead assigns the Yoma order to Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpa.
Another Yoma mishna places the lamp lottery before the incense lottery.
Abaye distinguishes cleaning two lamps from cleaning the first five.
But Abaye elsewhere puts the daily offering’s blood between the two lamp groups.
The differing sequences follow Abba Shaul and the Rabbis.
A baraita explicitly records their disagreement over whether lamps or incense come first.
What supports Abba Shaul’s sequence?
He reads the verse as putting lamp cleaning before incense.
How do the Rabbis interpret that same verse? The answer follows on the next side.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages read the verse as coordinating incense with lamp tending.
The analogous evening verse cannot require lighting before incense.
A baraita says the lamps burn from evening to morning and are the final evening service.
The evening verse means incense is offered at lamp-lighting time; the morning verse is read similarly.
Abba Shaul distinguishes the evening verse by its limiting word “it.”
Rav Pappa attributes the two contrary orders to the Sages and Abba Shaul.
Can the Yoma mishnayot really be assigned to those different teachers?
A later Yoma mishna again puts incense before lamp tending.
Rav Pappa accepts that the first and last clauses follow the Sages, with Abba Shaul in the middle.
Why does Rav Pappa reject Abaye’s reconciliation despite that awkward division?
On Abaye’s reading, the mishna mentions the last two lamps before the first five.
Abaye says the opening mishna teaches duties generally, while the detailed order appears later.
The discussion restates the dispute over sprinkling the daily offering’s blood at the altar corners.
What supports Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpa’s altered pattern?
The verse connects the daily burnt offering to a sin offering while preserving its identity as a burnt offering.
The blood is applied partly in the burnt-offering pattern and partly in the sin-offering pattern.
Why not complete both sets of sprinklings separately?
Blood cannot bring atonement twice.
Nor is it ordinary to make one blood application half a sin offering and half a burnt offering.
The verse nonetheless requires the two patterns to be linked.
Here the change is only division of an existing application.
Why not place the sin-offering pattern above the altar’s midpoint?
One offering’s blood is not usually divided between upper and lower zones.
The Holy of Holies blood application seems to include an upward and downward pattern.
Those applications form a descending line like lashes.
A sevenfold application on the inner altar might also cross its midpoint.
Rabba bar Sheila rejects that reading; his explanation continues next side.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The altar’s “purity” refers to its cleared upper surface, not its midpoint.
Why is the burnt-offering sprinkling performed before the sin-offering pattern?
The daily sacrifice is fundamentally a burnt offering, so its own rite comes first.
Why choose the northeast and southwest corners over southeast and northwest?
The southeast corner lacks the base needed for this sprinkling.
Why use the northeast corner before the southwest?
The priest turns rightward and meets the northeast corner first.
Could the verse instead modify the sin offering with a burnt-offering rite?
Its wording places a sin-offering feature on the daily burnt offering.
A mishna locates the Chamber of Lambs in the northwest of a four-chamber hall.
A mishna in Middot puts the Lamb Chamber in the southwest, creating a location conflict.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Middot locates the remaining chambers for shewbread, desecrated altar stones, and access to immersion.
Rav Huna attributes Middot to Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov to explain its different chamber locations.
A Middot description gives the women’s court dimensions and its southeast Nazirite chamber.
It places wood inspection by blemished priests in the northeast chamber.
It identifies the northwest lepers’ chamber and records Rabbi Eliezer’s uncertainty about the southwest chamber.
A second clue is Middot’s low eastern wall, allowing a view to the Sanctuary during red-heifer sprinkling.
Another mishna sets the Temple entrances at twenty cubits high.
The rampart and its stairs add six cubits of ascent.
Fifteen further stairs add seven and a half cubits.
Twelve stairs between hall and altar add six more cubits.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov adds a high step and a platform with further stairs.
With that added height the Sanctuary entrance is hidden from the eastern viewpoint.
Without it, half a cubit of the entrance would remain visible.
This appears to identify Middot with Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov.
Rav Adda offers Rabbi Yehuda’s centered altar as another explanation, continued next side.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda’s altar is centered on the Sanctuary entrance and could block its view.
Middot’s measurements challenge an attribution to Rabbi Yehuda.
The mishna totals the courtyard’s east-to-west dimensions and its principal spaces.
It also totals the north-to-south spaces around the ramp, altar, rings, tables, and pillars.
Those dimensions put most of the altar south of center, contrary to Rabbi Yehuda.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The measurements confirm that Middot follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov.
Rav Adda places the Lamb Chamber away from the corner so its apparent direction changes with the observer.
The chamber still appears closer to the southwest.
That inference follows from the parallel location problem for the shewbread chamber.
The two sources count the chambers in opposite directions around the hall.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Placing the Lamb Chamber southwest reconciles the two descriptions of the shewbread chamber.
A northwest Lamb Chamber would leave that conflict unresolved.
The Lamb Chamber therefore belongs nearer the southwest.
Does counting chambers leftward violate the rule to turn right?
That rule governs Temple service, not a descriptive count.
The mishna grants the High Priest first choice of offerings and portions.
A teaching illustrates his right to select a burnt or meal offering to sacrifice.
It illustrates his right to select sacrificial food and portions of festival loaves and shewbread.
Rabbi says he always receives five loaves, reading half the portion for Aaron.
The teaching appears internally inconsistent about half shares.
One of two loaves fits Rabbi’s half-share rule.
Four or five shewbread loaves fits the Sages instead.
The ending returns explicitly to Rabbi, producing an awkward alternation.
Abaye assigns the opening and middle to the Sages; they concede that a partial loaf is improper for the High Priest.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: When does the High Priest receive four loaves and when five?
On the Sages’ equal division between watches, he takes five, just under half of twelve.
On Rabbi Yehuda’s division, he takes four, just under half the ten available for sharing.
Rava reads the whole teaching as Rabbi’s view, raising why it permits four.
A delayed priestly watch receives two loaves, leaving eight to divide; without it ten remain.
The ending says Rabbi always takes five, contradicting that explanation.
The mishna says elders teach the High Priest the service and have him read it aloud.
They show him the sacrificial animals so he recognizes the work.
Food is unrestricted during preparation but limited near the fast to avoid sleepiness.
How could a High Priest have failed to learn the reading?
A teaching requires the High Priest to excel in strength, appearance, wisdom, and wealth.
Rav Yosef distinguishes standards in the First and Second Temple periods.
Marta’s payment for an appointment illustrates a less rigorous Second Temple process.
Another teaching includes goats among the animals shown to the priest.
Why does the mishna omit them?
Goats evoke sin and might distress him.
The bull is also a sin offering.
He knows his fellow priests and can prompt repentance, unlike the sins of all Israel.
Ravina cites a proverb about avoiding a familiar person who becomes an official.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Nekosa suggests flour and eggs to ease the fast-day bodily routine.
The Sages object that these foods can cause arousal and impurity.
A teaching lists foods and wines withheld from the High Priest to avoid an emission.
A parallel rule considers food as a possible cause of a zav’s emission and lists foods to avoid during examination.
The acrostics identify milk, cheese, egg, wine, beans, meat, and fish brine.
What does the general clause include?
It introduces another list of foods beginning with garlic, continued next side.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The food list continues, then introduces the biblical term for arugula.
Rabbi Meir identifies the biblical plant as arugula.
Why is it called by this name?
It is said to brighten the eyes.
Rav Huna recommends eating or applying arugula, and Rav Pappa specifies a field-edge variety.
Rav warns a guest against eggs and sleeping in the host’s garment.
Rav and Rav Nahman are described as announcing a temporary marriage when visiting towns.
A teaching warns that distant marriages can lead unwitting relatives to marry.
The Sages’ families were publicly known.
A newly consenting woman must wait seven clean days; how could same-day marriage occur?
Messengers announced the plan before the Sages arrived.
Alternatively, designation and seclusion supplied reassurance without consummating the union.
The mishna says priestly elders receive the High Priest, take him to the House of Avtinas, and administer an oath.
They require him to follow their instructions, and both sides weep after the oath.
Teaching or reading keeps him awake through the night.
They read Job, Ezra, Chronicles, or Daniel to him.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The House of Avtinas is used to teach the High Priest the incense handful.
Rav Pappa says the High Priest had two chambers, one north and one south.
A mishna enumerates three chambers on each side of the courtyard.
It describes the salt, Parva, and rinsing chambers on the south.
It identifies northern chambers, including a chamber associated with the High Priest.
The Exile Chamber supplied water for the courtyard.
The Chamber of Hewn Stone hosted review of priests’ fitness for service.
A description of the courtyard gates establishes the southern side and adjacent chambers.
It also identifies the northern gates and their watch posts.
The first of the High Priest’s five immersions occurred by the southern Water Gate, beside his chamber.
Which of his two chambers was the southern one?
The Parhedrin chamber seems more likely to have been in the south.
On that arrangement his morning and evening journeys for immersion and training are efficient.
A northern Parhedrin chamber would add tiring extra crossings of the courtyard.
Extra effort might intentionally discourage a Sadducee or prevent pride.
Otherwise the two chambers could simply have been placed together or replaced by one.
The mishna calls the High Priest the court’s agent.
That wording seems to challenge the view that serving priests act as God’s agents; the argument continues next side.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An agent cannot perform a rite forbidden to the appointing Israelite, supporting God’s agency for priests.
The oath means the priest must follow the court’s intended instructions.
The priest weeps at suspicion of Sadducee practice; the elders weep for possibly suspecting an innocent man.
Why was the oath so important?
It prevented preparing incense outside before entry to the Holy of Holies.
A Sadducee priest is said to have done exactly that, invoking the verse about appearing in a cloud.
The narrative reports his death or an angelic blow after the service.
Rav corrects a teacher’s pronunciation of Kevutal by gesturing.
Why not correct him aloud?
Rav was reciting Shema.
Teachings prohibit gesturing during Shema and compare it to failing to address God.
The prohibition applies to the first paragraph; Rav gestured in the second.
A teaching permits speech about sacred words during Shema but treats prayer more strictly.
Rabbi Aha says Torah should be a regular commitment.
Rava and Rav Aha bar Yaakov criticize idle chatter through biblical verses.
The mishna says young priests keep the High Priest awake by snapping and prompting movement.
Which finger is meant by tzerada?
Rav Yehuda identifies the finger opposed to the thumb, and Rav Huna demonstrates its sound.
The mishna’s prompt to stir on the floor is recalled.
Rav Yitzhak interprets it as asking for a difficult ceremonial bow.
The priests sing instead of using instruments and recite a verse about God building the house.
Jerusalem’s prominent people and others stayed awake to help the priest resist sleep.
Some gatherings led to wrongdoing.
A story about Nehardea illustrates the danger of Yom Kippur night gatherings.
Rav Yehuda asks what God said about those acts; the answer continues next side.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Elijah cites the verse describing sin at the doorway.
What did the accuser say?
Satan has no authority to accuse on Yom Kippur.
What is the basis for this?
The numerical value of “the Satan” is 364, leaving Yom Kippur outside his days of accusation.
The mishna gives ordinary, Yom Kippur, and festival times for removing altar ashes.
A mishna distinguishes sacrificial limbs fallen before and after midnight.
What establishes midnight as the dividing point?
Rav reconciles verses about all-night burning and ash removal by assigning each half the night.
Rav Kahana cites the variable ash-removal times in the mishna against a fixed midnight division.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If midnight were fixed by Torah law, ash removal could not vary before and after it.
Rabbi Yohanan reads the verse as allowing an early morning without fixing one hour.
On ordinary days removal occurs near the call of the gever.
On Yom Kippur it begins at midnight because of the High Priest’s workload.
On festivals it begins earlier because of crowds and offerings.
What is the call of the gever?
Rav says a man’s proclamation; Rabbi Sheila says a rooster’s crow.
Rav publicly explains the term as a man’s proclamation during Rabbi Sheila’s lesson.
Rabbi Sheila urges the rooster reading instead.
Rav cites earlier acceptance of his reading by Rabbi Hiyya.
Once identified, Rav declines to leave the teaching role, citing duty or rising sanctity.
Teachings are said to support each reading.
Gevini’s call to priests, Levites, and Israelites supports Rav.
King Agrippa heard the caller from three parasangs and rewarded him.
The High Priest’s call was reported audible at Jericho, ten parasangs away.
His voice carried despite fasting and daytime conditions.
Why is a voice harder to hear by day?
Rabbi Levi attributes it to the sound of the sun’s sphere and illustrates with visible dust.
A teaching contrasts the sounds of the sun’s sphere and Rome’s crowds.
Another teaching lists sounds said to travel across the world.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Another great sound is named, and prayer is said to have removed the sound of a soul’s departure.
A teaching using a rooster’s repeated call supports Rabbi Sheila’s meaning of gever.
Rav describes festival crowds that stand close but bow with space.
What does the eleven-cubit detail add?
Even an overflow behind the Holy of Holies had room to bow, counted as a Temple miracle.
A mishna lists miracles involving offerings, the High Priest, the crowd, and Jerusalem lodging.
The list ends with city miracles despite claiming ten Temple miracles.
Two Temple miracles involve rain not extinguishing the altar fire and wind not shifting its smoke.
Were there no further miracles?
Fragments and refuse from Temple service are described as sinking into the ground.
Three listed failures are counted together, allowing the other miracles into the tally.
If related events are merged, the sinking events should also count as one.
Bread remaining warm from placement to removal supplies another miracle.
Were there still no other Temple miracles?
Traditions say the Ark and cherubs fit in spaces too narrow by ordinary measurement.
The list counts visible outer miracles and excludes inner Sanctuary miracles.
The shewbread miracle also seems to occur inside.
The shewbread could be seen outside; an argument from the table’s purity begins here.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: How can a fixed wooden table be susceptible to impurity?
The table was lifted for pilgrims to see the shewbread still warm after a week.
Were there no more Temple miracles?
A tradition describes golden Temple trees producing fruit until the Sanctuary was invaded.
Perpetual miracles, including those of Ark and cherubs, are excluded from the list.
How could altar fire produce smoke if the heavenly fire was smokeless?
A teaching lists five qualities of that heavenly fire, including its lack of smoke.
The smoky fire was the additional fire brought by priests.
Was the heavenly fire lion-shaped or dog-shaped?
The lion belongs to the First Temple and the dog to the Second.
A teaching lists the heavenly fire among five phenomena absent from the Second Temple.
Some fire existed there, but it did not assist the altar service.
A baraita classifies six forms of fire by what they consume or repel.
It identifies ordinary, fever, Elijah’s, altar, Gabriel’s, and divine fire.
Could winds really not shift the altar smoke?
The smoke’s direction on the last festival day was read as a weather omen.
The column swayed in the wind but did not scatter.
The omen associates eastward smoke with joy and westward smoke with sorrow.
Another teaching assesses east, west, north, and south winds differently for crops.
The table and lamp positions serve as a mnemonic for wheat and olives.
The wind rules apply to different regions, Babylonia and the Land of Israel.
The first chapter concludes.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Initially any priest could clear the ashes; when several came, a race up the ramp decided.
A tie was settled by counting one or two raised fingers, without thumbs.
A dangerous shove and broken leg led the court to institute the first of four daily lotteries.
Why was a lottery not instituted from the outset?
The Sages expected little interest in night work until crowding and danger proved otherwise.
Burning limbs and fats also occurs at night but had a lottery.
That burning completes daytime sacrificial service.
Ash removal might likewise start the coming day’s service, as Rabbi Yohanan’s hand-washing rule suggests.
His wording can instead mean washing before a service, without defining ash removal as daytime work.
Another explanation says the Sages expected sleepiness to keep priests away, then saw danger instead.
Nighttime burning also faces sleepiness yet has a lottery.
Remaining awake late differs from waking early.
Did the dangerous race alone cause the lottery rule?
The ash winner also gained wood-arranging duties, which could warrant a lottery.
Rav Ashi says the first enactment established a lottery after danger.
A second enactment added wood duties after the lottery reduced participation.
The mishna’s crowded-race rule is recalled.
Rav Pappa excludes ground-level four cubits.
He also excludes the first four cubits of the ramp.
Unmarked middle cubits cannot be the decisive area.
The four cubits nearest the altar are meant.
Does the measured area include the altar base and ledge? The question continues next side.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The four-cubit measurement might exclude the altar base and ledge; the question remains open.
Tied priests are told to extend fingers for the lottery count.
Why not count the priests themselves?
Rabbi Yitzhak prohibits directly numbering Israelites, citing Saul’s count by objects.
Rav Ashi says Bezek could be a place name rather than pieces used for counting.
Another verse explicitly counts Saul’s people through sheep.
Rabbi Elazar and Rav Nahman infer one or two prohibitions on counting Israel.
How can Israel have a number yet be uncountable?
One reading distinguishes times of obedience from disobedience.
Another distinguishes counting by humans from counting by Heaven.
Shmuel says a public leader becomes wealthy, illustrated by Saul’s later count with sheep.
Perhaps the sheep belonged to the people.
That would make the reported method unremarkable.
Rabbi Mani reads Saul’s struggle in the valley as debate over the command against Amalek.
Saul questions destruction of many lives, animals, and children.
A divine voice warns against excessive righteousness.
Later, when Saul orders priests killed, a divine voice warns against excessive wickedness.
Rav Huna contrasts Saul’s lost reign after one sin with David’s retained reign after two.
Was Saul’s action against the priests of Nob not another sin?
The loss of kingship was already decreed after Agag.
Which two sins of David are in view?
Uriah’s death and the census are named.
What about Bathsheba?
That act drew a distinct fourfold punishment.
The census also brought a separate plague.
David was not punished personally for the census.
The Bathsheba punishment also appears to affect others.
Rav says David himself suffered illness, isolation, and loss of divine presence.
Rav also says David accepted slander about Mephibosheth.
Shmuel denies that David accepted a false report.
Even on Rav’s view, the later split of the kingdom punishes that judgment separately.
Rav Huna reads Saul as morally unblemished like a one-year-old at accession.
Rav Nahman offers a disparaging alternative reading.
After troubling dreams, he twice apologizes to Saul with greater respect.
Why did Saul’s dynasty not endure?
His lineage had no blemish that could restrain a leader’s arrogance.
Why was Saul punished further?
He let early public contempt for his kingship pass without asserting royal authority.
A further maxim about Torah scholars begins and continues next side.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

An objection from a story: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ate figs and grapes outside the sukka, and the inference drawn is that fixed meals need a sukka.

Alternatively, the fruit was a fixed meal and bread eaten with it was a casual snack, both outside the sukka.
The Gemara proposes a baraita as support for Rava: one fulfills sukka with sweets, which may include fruit.
The support fails: the baraita's sweets mean fruit, or it refers to places where fruit is scarce.
Rav Zevid holds that the large date is less than an egg-bulk.
Rav Zevid cites a mishna: Beit Shammai measure leaven at an olive-bulk and leavened bread at a large date.
What is the reason for Beit Shammai's view?
If the Torah had one measure for both, it would have written only chametz; the Gemara's reasoning is offered.
A kal vachomer: if chametz is forbidden at a small quantity, leaven, which leavens more strongly, should be forbidden at least as easily.
Since the Torah names both leaven and leavened bread, the measures differ: an olive-bulk for leaven, a large date for leavened bread.
Beit Shammai's ruling: an olive-bulk of leaven and a large date's volume of leavened bread.
If the large date exceeded an egg-bulk, Beit Shammai would have taught an egg-bulk, so the date must be smaller than an egg.
Rejects the inference: Beit Shammai meant a normal date, or the two measures are equal and one was chosen.
Zimmun: Rabbi Meir says an olive-bulk obligates those eating together, Rabbi Yehuda says an egg-bulk.
What do Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda actually disagree about?
Rabbi Meir reads the verse's eating and satisfaction as an olive-bulk, defining eating by the Torah's usage.
Rabbi Yehuda reads Deuteronomy 8:10 as eating that satisfies, which requires an egg-bulk.
If a large date were above an egg-bulk, an egg-bulk would satisfy yet not settle the mind; so the date must be smaller.
A baraita is introduced, attributing a teaching to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

ranges.en: All Torah eating measures are an olive-bulk, except impurity of food, where the verse's wording led the Sages to a different measure.
The Gemara offers Yom Kippur as proof that a change in the verse's wording yields a different measure.
How did the Sages learn from the verse that its wording changed the measure?
Leviticus 23:29, 'any soul which shall not be afflicted', is cited as the scriptural basis.
How did the Sages change the measure for the prohibition on Yom Kippur?
The prohibition applies only to eating a large date-bulk rather than an olive-bulk.
What is the proof for this from Yom Kippur, since impurity alone should suffice?
Impurity alone might be dismissed as the verse's style, so Yom Kippur teaches that wording changes halakha.
From where do we derive that the impurity measure of food is an egg-bulk?
Rabbi Elazar cites Leviticus 11:34, 'of all food which may be eaten', with the doubled root as teaching food from food.
The food that comes from food is a chicken egg.
Objection: say it means a kid, which also comes from a mother.
A kid is not yet food until ritually slaughtered, so it is excluded.
Objection: say it means a ben pekua, a calf born from a slaughtered mother.
The calf still requires cutting, though not ritual slaughter, so it is excluded.
Objection: the measure may be the giant egg of the bar yokhani bird.
In doubt take the smaller number, so the measure is a chicken egg.
Objection: say it means a very small bird's egg, so no proof is decisive.
Rabbi Abbahu reads 'of all food which may be eaten' as food eaten at one time.
The Sages estimated that the throat cannot hold more than a chicken egg's volume, so that is the measure.
Rabbi Elazar rules that one who unwittingly eats forbidden fat must record the measure, lest a later court raise it.
What does it mean that a later court might increase the measure?
If a later court made liability begin at a small olive, the sinner would not be liable for an offering; the baraita says otherwise.
Leviticus 4:22 and a baraita: only one who repents upon awareness of his sin brings an offering for unwitting sin.
Rather, a court might require the bulk of a large olive, so one should record the amount eaten.
Recalls the first suggestion: a later court might lower the measure to a small olive's bulk.
What is the meaning of increase in measures, if Rabbi Elazar should have said decrease?
The increase may refer to more offerings brought because the measure for liability was reduced.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says measures and punishments are a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.
Objection: the punishments are written explicitly in the Torah, so they cannot be oral transmission.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's statement is corrected: only the measures that determine liability for punishments come from Sinai.
A baraita teaches that the measures of punishments are halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.
Others say these measures were instituted by the court of Jabez.
Objection: Leviticus 27:34 says a prophet may not innovate anything, so Jabez's court could not have instituted them.
The measures were forgotten and later restored by the prophets, not newly invented.
Mishna: one who drinks a cheekful is liable; Shmuel reads it as the appearance of a cheekful pushed to one side.
Objection: the mishna says 'a cheekful' in the plural, which implies two actual cheeks full.
Say instead: like the appearance of a cheekful, as seen from one side.
Objection from a baraita: Beit Shammai say a quarter-log, Beit Hillel say a cheekful.
The baraita reports Rabbi Yehuda in Rabbi Eliezer's name (a cheekful in appearance), and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira (a single gulp).
Is the baraita preferable to the mishna?
The baraita may be read like the mishna: an amount that looks like a cheekful.
If so, Beit Hillel match Rabbi Eliezer, who also says like two cheeks full.
The difference lies in a paltry cheekful: Beit Hillel require a full one, Rabbi Eliezer obligates even less.
Rav Hoshaya objects: this makes Beit Hillel's measure the lenient one, which Eduyyot would have recorded.
The reply begins here, 'He said to him,' and is cut off at the end of the daf.

ranges.en: Clarifies that the liquid-measure question concerns even Og king of Bashan, whose cheekful is large, so Beit Shammai are stringent.
Rabbi Zeira objects: eating has one fixed measure for all, so why should drinking be measured by each person's own mouth?
Abaye replies: the tradition fixes the eating measure by settling the mind, while drinking settles each person by his own cheekful.
Rabbi Zeira objects again: if eating is measured by mind-settling, why is Og's large-date measure the same as everyone's?
Abaye replies: the tradition fixes the measure; average people are greatly satisfied, Og only a little, yet the measure relieves all.
Rabbi Zeira objects: fatty meat and grapevine shoots should differ in satisfying the mind at the same measure.
Abaye replies: the measure is fixed by tradition; fatty meat satisfies greatly, grapevine shoots only a little.
Rava objects: the eating measure is an olive-bulk in half a loaf's time, so the Yom Kippur large-date measure is an unexplained leniency.
Abaye replies: the time limit is fixed by tradition, since eating within it settles the mind and eating over longer does not.
Rava objects: the impurity measure of two egg-bulks in half a loaf's time is far larger, so why is the Yom Kippur case different?
Rav Pappa replies: impurity of the body from food is only rabbinic, and the Sages were lenient, so it need not be raised here.
Objection: Rav Pappa elsewhere holds from Leviticus 11:43 that bodily impurity from food is Torah law.
Rav Pappa did not mean Torah law; the law is rabbinic and the verse is only a support.
Mishna: all foods combine for the Yom Kippur measure; Rav Pappa says meat and the salt on it combine to a large date.
Reish Lakish: brine on a vegetable combines with it to reach a large date for Yom Kippur eating.
The Gemara finds this obvious; it asks why brine should not combine, since it is food, and suggests it might be a drink.
The Gemara concludes that anything that prepares food for eating is itself considered food.
Reish Lakish: one who eats excessively on Yom Kippur, beyond satiety, is exempt.
The reason: Leviticus 23:29 'shall not be afflicted' excludes one who harms himself through excess.
Rabbi Yirmeya, citing Reish Lakish: a non-priest who eats teruma excessively pays the principal but not the added fifth.
Leviticus 22:14, 'if a man eat', excludes the one who harms himself rather than eating normally.
Rabbi Yirmeya, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, begins a further statement about a non-priest who eats teruma.

ranges.en: Raw teruma barley eaten unground pays only the principal, not the added fifth.
A verse about eating is cited to exclude one who harms himself.
Rav Sheizvi reports Rabbi Yochanan's case of a non-priest who swallowed and vomited teruma plums.
The second person who ate the vomited plums pays only the fuel value to the first.
Eating and drinking do not combine to reach the liability measure.
Asks who the tanna is behind this ruling.
Rav Chisda says the ruling is a dispute and follows Rabbi Yehoshua.
Mishna citing Rabbi Yehoshua's principle on which impurity measures combine.
Rav Nachman: even by the Rabbis, combining applies to impurity only, not to Yom Kippur measures.
Reish Lakish likewise says the question is a dispute, following Rabbi Yehoshua.
Reish Lakish cites the same mishna principle as support.
Rabbi Yochanan repeats Rav Nachman's reasoning about settling the mind.
Mishna: one lapse of awareness gives one sin-offering; separate prohibitions give two; unfit items are exempt.
Why does the Torah state no explicit warning against afflicting oneself on Yom Kippur?
It could not be phrased that way; the proposed wordings would mean eating or rising.
Rav Hoshaya proposes writing a guard-lest-not-afflicted formulation instead.
Then there would be too many negative prohibitions in the verse.
Rav Beivai proposes writing a guard formulation within the affliction mitzva.
Guard wording attached to a mitzva signals a positive command, not a prohibition.
Rav Ashi proposes writing a do-not-stray-from-affliction formulation.
The Gemara concedes the objection is difficult, though it could have been written so.
A tanna derives the affliction prohibitions from Numbers 29:7 and the labor verse.
Baraita: one might think labor during the extension would be punishable by karet.
The verse teaches karet only for labor on the day itself, not during the extension.
One might think labor-extension is not karet but affliction-extension is.
The verse cited makes karet apply to not afflicting on the day itself.
Conclusion: karet applies on the day itself, not to affliction in the extension.
One might think no lashes for extension labor; the labor verse is then cited.
The verse says labor is forbidden on that very day, showing warning only for the day.
Warned for the day but not for extension labor; one might think affliction-extension is warned.
A fortiori: labor observed on Shabbat is not warned in the extension, so affliction, not observed, is not either.
Where is the warning for affliction on the day itself derived from?
Karet for labor can be inferred a fortiori from karet for affliction.
Why then is the karet for labor explicitly stated?
It is free for a verbal analogy linking karet for affliction and labor.
Verbal analogy: labor's warning and punishment work the same, so affliction does too.
Affliction has no permitted exceptions, unlike labor, so the analogy is refuted.
Rather, learn karet for affliction a fortiori from labor's karet, which has exceptions.
A fortiori argument applied to the verse's karet wording.
Why is the phrase stated if it is available for analogy?
It is available for a verbal analogy linking karet in both affliction and labor.
Analogy: labor is punished only after warning, so affliction likewise.
Labor is observed on Shabbat and festivals while affliction is not, so the analogy fails.
Ravina: the baraita's verbal analogy from on that same day is needed to teach this.
The Gemara replies it is available; five verses are written for labor on Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Yishmael's school derives it by verbal analogy from affliction in the rape context.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives it from the verbal analogy of Shabbat of solemn rest.
Rav Pappa introduces a further statement, cut off here.

ranges.en: Yom Kippur is called Shabbat; a verse about the day itself is preferred over an analogy.
Why did Rav Aha bar Yaakov not state his view the way Rav Pappa did?
A baraita reconciles the fast beginning at evening with the ninth day, adding time from weekday to holy.
Baraita derives that time is added at the start and end of Yom Kippur, Festivals and Shabbatot.
What does the tanna who derives from that same day do with on the ninth day?
He requires it, as Hiyya bar Rav of Difti taught in a baraita.
Hiyya's baraita: eating on the ninth and fasting on the tenth earns credit as fasting both days.
Mishna exempts eating unfit food; Rava says raw pepper and ginger are exempt.
Rabbi Meir's verse shows pepper is food subject to orla, contradicting Rava.
Edible pepper is fresh and moist; the Yom Kippur halakha concerns dry pepper.
Ravina cites Rav Nachman permitting cooked ginger, implying ginger is food.
Wet ginger is food; the Yom Kippur ruling refers to dry ginger.
Baraita: leaves of reeds are exempt, but grapevine shoots are liable.
What are these grapevine shoots?
Rabbi Yitzhak of Migdal says shoots sprouted before Yom Kippur count as food; Rav Kahana says thirty days.
A baraita is cited in line with Rabbi Yitzhak of Migdal's definition of shoots.
Mishna exempts drinking brine; by implication drinking vinegar is liable.
Which tanna stands behind the mishna's ruling?
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: vinegar revives the spirit, so it counts as a beverage.
Rav Giddel rules against Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; people drink vinegar anyway, and he is angered.
Rav Giddel clarifies his ruling: only after the fact, only small amounts, only pure vinegar.

ranges.en: Mishna: children are not made to fast on Yom Kippur but are trained one or two years before maturity.
Why does the mishna say one year when two years already covers it?
Rav Chisda: the one-year ruling refers to a feeble child, the two-year ruling to a healthy child.
Rav Huna: healthy children at eight and nine are trained; from twelve they complete the fast by Torah law.
Rav Nachman sets the ages differently, with boys completing the fast at thirteen by Torah law.
Rabbi Yochanan: there is no rabbinic completion; girls complete the fast by Torah law at twelve.
The mishna is cited: children are trained one or two years before maturity.
Rav Huna and Rav Nachman's reading works, but Rabbi Yochanan's reading is difficult.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that one or two years means the period right before maturity.
A baraita of Rabba bar Shmuel supports the one-or-two-year training rule.
The baraita works for Rabbi Yochanan but is difficult for Rav Huna and Rav Nachman.
The Rabbis reply that the training refers to completing a full fast day by rabbinic law.
Is training really called completion, since training means only part of the mitzva?
A baraita illustrates training: feeding a child at a later hour each time.
Rava bar Ulla: these are two types of training, brief waiting for small children and full-day fasting for older ones.
Mishna: pregnant or ill persons are fed until they recover, guided by experts or by their own word.
Baraita: a pregnant woman craving forbidden food is given increasingly direct forms; only idolatry, incest and bloodshed override life.
From where do we derive that the prohibition of idolatry overrides saving one's life?
Rabbi Eliezer derives the hierarchy from the three phrases of the love verse.
From where do we derive the rule for bloodshed and sexual prohibitions?
Rabbi cites the verse about a man who rises against his fellow and slays him.
What is the point of comparing the murderer to the betrothed girl, whose halakha is already clear?
The comparison actually teaches something new, reversing the inference from the murderer.
Deduction: the betrothed girl may be saved at the attacker's cost, and one must die rather than transgress.

ranges.en: From where is the murderer's own halakha derived, that he must die rather than kill?
It is derived by reason, as shown in a case brought before Rava.
Rava's reasoning: your blood is not redder than his, so you may not kill another to save yourself.
A pregnant woman craves food on Yom Kippur; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says whisper that it is the fast day, and it works.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reads a Jeremiah verse about the child in the womb to explain the outcome.
The child born to that woman was Rabbi Yochanan.
A second story: Rabbi Chanina's whisper fails, the woman keeps craving, and he reads a verse about the baby.

ranges.en: Psalm verse cited that the wicked are estranged from the womb; Shabbetai the hoarder is an example.
Mishna: a sick person who needs food is fed on the advice of experts.
Rabbi Yannai: if the sick person says he needs food and a doctor disagrees, listen to the sick person.
What is the reason, and is it not obvious that a person knows his own pain?
Lest one think a doctor's experience is more reliable, the verse teaches that the sick person knows best.
Reverse case: if a doctor says he needs food but the sick person refuses, listen to the doctor.
Confusion has taken hold of the sick person, so his judgment is impaired.
The mishna's wording implies experts override the patient and that two experts are needed, contrary to Rabbi Yannai.
The case is one where the sick person says he does not need food.
Let them feed him on one expert's advice, as Rabbi Yannai said.
If so, it is obvious, since uncertainty about life is decided leniently.
No: two experts are required when a third disagrees; majority rule applies to testimony, not to life-risk.
Since the latter clause feeds him on his own word if no experts are present, the first clause must mean he wants food.
The mishna is incomplete: the experts' ruling applies only if he says he does not need food.
Mar bar Rav Ashi: if the sick person says he needs food, follow him even against one hundred doctors.
The mishna's latter clause seems to imply that experts would override the sick person if present.
Rejected: the experts' ruling applies only when the sick person says he does not need food.
Mishna: a bulmos patient may eat impure food; Rabbi Matya ben Harash disputes the mad-dog liver remedy.
Rabbi Matya ben Harash: a possible throat danger overrides Shabbat for medicine placed in the mouth.
Mishna: rescue from a rockslide under every uncertainty; if found dead, leave him.
From where would they know that his sight has recovered?
Recovery is shown by distinguishing good from bad food; Abaye says by tasting.
Baraita: feed the least severe prohibition first, such as neveila before untithed produce.
The tanna'im dispute whether untithed produce or teruma is fed first.
Rabbah: where non-sacred food can be made by tithing, do so even on Shabbat.
First Sage: untithed produce is more severe, since teruma is fit for priests.
Second Sage: teruma is more severe, since untithed produce can be made fit.

ranges.en: Rabba: if untithed produce can be made fit, the ill person should eat non-sacred food after tithing.
Is it not obvious that one should tithe if possible? Why state it?
On Shabbat the prohibition is only moving, which is rabbinic, so surely it is lighter than eating untithed produce.
The case is fruit grown in an imperforate pot, untithed only by rabbinic law, so one tithes on Shabbat.
The two sages disagree: one holds untithed produce is more severe, the other holds teruma is more severe.
Baraita on a snake-bitten patient on Shabbat: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allows untithed leeks; Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon requires tithing.
Suggests Rabba follows Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rejected: Rabba can follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who exempts only rabbinic vegetable tithes, not grain tithes.
Baraita: honey and sweets restore sight in bulmos; Jonathan's words in Samuel allude to this.
Why say there is no clear proof when Jonathan's verse seems to prove it?
Abaye: honey restores sight only after a meal, and the verse about the Egyptian shows sweets come after the main course.
Rav Nachman in Shmuel's name: a sheep's tail with honey is a remedy for bulmos.
Rav Huna: fine wheat flour with honey is a remedy.
Rav Pappa: even barley flour with honey helps.
Rabbi Yochanan's experience of eating ripe figs on the east side, supported by Ecclesiastes 7:12.
Rav Yosef's teaching: one who wants fig flavor should face east, since the sun ripens fruit.
Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei: one robbed a shepherd in bulmos, while the other robbed a whole city.
Rabbi Meir analyzes names; the travelers meet an innkeeper named Kidor and hand over their purses.
Meir infers wickedness from the name Kidor, citing the verse about a generation of upheavals.
Yehuda and Yosei hand over their purses; Meir hides his at the innkeeper's father's grave.
The innkeeper's father appears in a dream; Meir does not trust it but guards the purse all day.
The innkeeper denies the deposit; Meir explains he only warned of suspicion, not certain wickedness.
The travelers trap the innkeeper with lentils on his mustache; in anger he kills his wife.
Parallel baraita on laxity in hand washing that led to pork, cited against the innkeeper story.
They also test names: a landlord named Bala is judged wicked by the verse about adultery and age.
Mishna: one bitten by a mad dog is not fed its liver lobe; the mad dog's nature is then examined.
Baraita lists five signs of a mad dog, including an open mouth, dripping saliva and roaming roads.
From where did the dog become mad?
Rav: witches practice magic on it; Shmuel: an evil spirit rests upon it.
What is the practical difference between these two opinions?

ranges.en: Rest of a ruling: a mad dog is killed only with a thrown object, not by hand.
Baraita in line with Shmuel: kill a mad dog only with a thrown object; being rubbed by it is dangerous, being bitten fatal.
What is the remedy for one who was rubbed by a mad dog?
Take off the clothing and run; Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua did so in the market.
Rav Huna cites Ecclesiastes 7:12: wisdom preserves the lives of those who have it.
What is the remedy for one bitten by a mad dog, who will die?
Abaye: a hyena-skin spell, buried clothing for twelve months, and drinking only from copper tubes.
The mishna on Matya ben Harash's permission of medicine in the mouth on Shabbat is cited.
Rabbi Yochanan learns a cure for tzefidna from a gentile matron after an oath, then publicizes it.
Did he not swear not to reveal it? The vow is read narrowly, and the remedy was already revealed to her.
What medicine did the matron prepare for him?
Rav Acha son of Rav Ami: leaven-steeped water, olive oil and salt.
Rav Yeimar: leaven itself, olive oil and salt.
Rav Ashi: fat from the marrow of a goose wing.
Abaye tried these without cure, then was healed by an Arab's remedy of burnt unripe olive seeds.
Tzefidna comes from hot bread and fried fish; its sign is blood from the gums when touched.
How did Rabbi Yochanan prepare the medicine on Shabbat for a gum ailment that is not life-threatening?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: tzefidna begins in the mouth but ends in the intestines, so it is dangerous.
In accordance with whose opinion did Rabbi Yochanan act, given that Rabbi Matya's view is a minority?
Rabbi Yochanan: the Sages agreed with Rabbi Matya only in this case, so his view is not a minority here.
A baraita attributed to Rabbi Matya lists permitted remedies, including mouth medicine on Shabbat.
Do the Rabbis' words excluding these items also exclude the tzefidna medicine?
No: they exclude bloodletting for serunkhi, which Rabbi Matya permits on Shabbat.
Baraita: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei reports three things he heard from Rabbi Matya ben Harash.
Then what do the Rabbis exclude, if not bloodletting, which everyone agrees is effective?
No proof: the Rabbis' exclusion refers only to the first two items of the earlier baraita.

ranges.en: Baraita of Rabba bar Shmuel: feed a pregnant woman, use the mad-dog liver, and give mouth medicine on Shabbat, per Rabbi Matya ben Harash.
To which case does the Rabbis' limitation refer? A pregnant woman is obvious, so it must concern Shabbat medicine.
Rav Ashi: the mishna's structure shows the Rabbis do not dispute Rabbi Matya's ruling on medicine.
Why state that uncertainty of life overrides Shabbat, when this is already known?
Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: the principle covers even uncertainty about a different, future Shabbat.
What circumstances create uncertainty about danger on a future Shabbat?
A doctor's eight-day treatment beginning on Shabbat: act immediately, though another Shabbat is desecrated.
Baraita: heat water for the ill on Shabbat immediately, even for uncertainty about a future Shabbat.
Only scholars may decide such acts on Shabbat, not gentiles, Samaritans or women, though their views combine in disputes.
Baraita: one saving a life on Shabbat need not seek a court's permission, as in rescuing a child from sea or pit.
Baraita: breaking a locked door or barring a fire to save a child or life, also without court permission.
Why teach each example? Each adds a distinct case that a delay would not seem to justify.
The pit case alone might seem justified by fear, so the locked door case is taught as well.
Why state the fire barrier case, which seems already covered by the life-danger principle?
It applies even if the fire threatens to spread to an adjacent courtyard.
Shmuel in Rav Yehuda's name: in saving life the Sages did not follow the majority rule.
Under which circumstances would the majority not apply? Nine Jews with one gentile, or an even split, are problematic.
Alternatively, nine gentiles and one Jew: a fixed group is treated as evenly divided.
The majority is not followed when an individual separated from a group and debris fell on him.
Rav Asi cites Rabbi Yochanan: debris removal differs by courtyard, which seems to contradict Shmuel.
No contradiction: in one case all left, so uncertainty remains; in the other only some left.
Did Shmuel really say this? The mishna on an abandoned child follows the city's majority.
Rav: the majority determines only sustenance, not lineage, so the child's marital status remains uncertain.

ranges.en: Shmuel's ruling on clearing rubble for a foundling, and the context in which it was said.
Shmuel's ruling is clarified as applying only to the first halakha, the foundling's status.
Shmuel holds that for saving a life the rule is different; one relies on uncertainty.
Baraita: in a gentile-majority city the foundling has gentile status.
Asks which halakha this gentile-status ruling actually affects.
It affects feeding the foundling non-kosher food, as Rav Pappa explains.
Baraita continuation: in a Jewish-majority city the foundling is a Jew.
Asks which halakha the Jewish-majority ruling affects.
It affects the obligation to return a lost object to him.
Baraita: in an equal mixed city the foundling is treated as a Jew.
Asks which halakha the equal-city ruling applies to.
Reish Lakish: it applies to damage halakhot, such as an ox goring.
Asks what the concrete case of the damage ruling looks like.
If our ox gored his, he would have to prove he is Jewish before claiming, so no claim.
Rather, the case is his innocuous ox goring ours; he pays half and the foundling need not prove status.
Mishnah: one clears rubble from one who may be under it, possibly alive, possibly Jewish.
Asks what the mishnah means by listing three uncertainties.
Needless-to-say reading: each uncertainty is a stronger case than the one before, so clearing is required.
Mishnah: if they found him alive, they keep clearing the rubble.
Asks why this is needed, since saving a living person is obvious.
It is needed to show clearing continues even if he will only live a short while.
Mishnah: if they found him dead, they leave him where he is.
Asks why this is needed, since it seems obvious.
It is needed to rule out that concern for a corpse permits desecrating Shabbat.
Reish Lakish's view is cited via a baraita: one may not save a corpse from a fire on Shabbat.
Reish Lakish's own report: one may save a corpse from a fire.
Limit Reish Lakish: he refers only to a fire, where the mourner might extinguish it; here no such risk.
Baraita: one checks for life until the nose, or as some say, the heart, and must not assume the lower are dead.
Story: they found the upper victims dead but the lower ones alive.
Suggests the dispute about signs of life mirrors the tanna dispute about fetal formation.
Baraita: a fetus is formed from the head, according to the first tanna.
Psalm 71:6 uses the word gozi, meaning from the mother womb, to support the head view.
Jeremiah 7:29 uses gozi for cutting hair, to support the head view again.
Abba Shaul: a fetus is formed from the navel and sends roots outward.
Even if Abba Shaul holds the navel view, he may still require checking the nose.
Abba Shaul spoke only of formation; for saving life he agrees that breath resides in the nose.
Genesis 7:22 says all in whose nostrils was the breath of life, showing breath is in the nose.
Rav Pappa: the dispute concerns digging from below; from above, once the nose is checked, one stops.
Genesis 7:22 again supports that once the nose is checked, no further checking is needed.
Story setup: R. Yishmael, R. Akiva and R. Elazar ben Azarya walk ahead while the younger students follow.
The question of whether saving life overrides Shabbat is asked before the teachers.
Asks from where it is derived that saving a life overrides Shabbat.
R. Yishmael answers with a verse.
Exodus 22:1 on a thief: if one may kill a thief to save property, the a fortiori applies to life.
Kal vachomer: saving a life overrides Shabbat, so R. Yishmael's conclusion stands.
R. Akiva answers with another verse.
Exodus 21:14 about a murderer taken from the altar, showing a priest is removed to be executed.
Rabba bar bar Hana cites R. Yohanan: they taught only that a priest is not taken down from the altar to be killed.

ranges.en: But to save a life one removes even a priest from atop the altar during service.
A fortiori: the priest is removed from service to save life, so life overrides Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya answers the question.
A fortiori from circumcision, which overrides Shabbat, to saving the whole body.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda holds that Shabbat is kept except where life is at stake.
The word but in the verse Keep my Shabbatot restricts the general command.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef offers a different reading of the verse.
For it is sacred to you shows Shabbat is given into your hands, not you to it.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya gives his view.
Keep Shabbat verse: the Torah lets one Shabbat be desecrated so many may be kept.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: Shmuel's own proof from live by them is superior to theirs.
Leviticus 18:5 says live by them, not die by them, supporting Shmuel.
Rava: all these arguments have refutations except Shmuel's, which has none.
R. Yishmael's thief proof could be refuted by Rava's principle about the thief.
Rava's reasoning: a person does not defend his money, so the thief kills out of fear and the Torah permits self-defense.
Asks from where we derive saving a life in uncertain danger, not only certain danger.
R. Akiva's proof can likewise be refuted, following Abaye's position.
Abaye: we send rabbis to check whether the accused's witness has substance before removing the priest.
Asks the same question for uncertain danger in Abaye's case.
All the other proofs bring only certain danger, so they are refuted for uncertainty.
Shmuel's proof has no refutation, since it covers even uncertain danger.
Ravina, or Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: Shmuel's proof is like a spicy pepper, better than a basket of squash.
Mishna: sin-offerings, guilt-offerings, death, and Yom Kippur atone, and repentance atones for minor sins and places severe sins in abeyance.
Mishna: one who plans to sin and repent, or to rely on Yom Kippur, gets no atonement; Yom Kippur atones only between man and God, not man and man.
R. Elazar ben Azarya teaches the same point from the verse.
Leviticus 16:30: from all your sins you shall be cleansed before the Lord.
Exposition: Yom Kippur atones for sins between man and God, but not man and man until one appeases the other.
R. Akiva: how fortunate Israel is, purified by their Father in Heaven.
Ezekiel 36:25 on sprinkling pure water and being purified supports the point.
Jeremiah 17:13: the ritual bath of Israel is God, who purifies as a ritual bath does.
Gemara: the mishna says a definite guilt-offering atones, implying an uncertain one does not.
Asks why not, since atonement is written regarding the uncertain guilt-offering.
Those offerings give full atonement, while the uncertain one gives only temporary atonement until the sin is known.
Alternatively, Yom Kippur atones for the uncertain guilt-offering in a way it does not for the others.
A mishna: if Yom Kippur passed, those liable for sin-offerings still owe them, but uncertain guilt-offering owners are exempt.
The mishna says death and Yom Kippur atone only with repentance.
Without repentance, they do not atone on their own.
Perhaps the mishna is not like Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose view is cited next.
Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: Yom Kippur atones for all Torah sins with repentance, except rejecting Torah and a few grave sins.
Rejected: even on his view, repentance is needed to complete atonement, while Yom Kippur needs no repentance.
Mishna: repentance itself atones for minor sins, both positive and negative commandments.
Asks why positive mitzva is taught if repentance already atones for negative mitzva.
Rav Yehuda: the mishna means a negative mitzva whose violation can be fixed by a positive act, not a full negative mitzva.
Asks whether repentance does not atone for a full negative mitzva.
Raises a contradiction from a baraita listing minor transgressions as positive and negative mitzvot.

ranges.en: The exception is the prohibition of taking God's name in vain and any similar severe prohibition.
Proposes a baraita from Rabbi Yehuda as a contrary source.
Rabbi Yehuda: repentance atones below the name-in-vain prohibition; repentance suspends and Yom Kippur atones above it.
Rejected: it may refer to the name-in-vain prohibition and anything similar.
Another source: since repentance and absolving were said at Horeb, perhaps even name-in-vain is included.
The verse's wording shows God does not absolve name-in-vain, though he absolves other prohibitions.
The Gemara resolves it as a dispute between tanna'im.
Baraita: repentance atones positive and rectifiable negative commandments; Yom Kippur atones karet, death penalty, and full negatives.
Clarifying the baraita: the Master cited the Horeb verse about repentance and absolving.
Asks from where we derive that repentance is mentioned at Horeb.
R. Elazar: absolve and will not absolve cannot both apply to everything, so God absolves only those who repent.
R. Matya ben Harash asks R. Elazar ben Azarya in Rome about four categories of atonement taught by R. Yishmael.
R. Elazar replies that there are three categories, and repentance is needed for each.
Positive commandment violated and repented: forgiven immediately, before leaving the spot.
Jeremiah 3:22 supports immediate forgiveness for one who repents.
Prohibition violated: repentance suspends punishment and Yom Kippur atones.
Leviticus 16:30 supports Yom Kippur atoning for prohibitions.
Karet or death-penalty sins: repentance and Yom Kippur suspend, and suffering completes the atonement.
Psalms 89:33 supports suffering absolving through punishment.
Desecration of God's name: repentance, Yom Kippur, and suffering cannot absolve; only death does.
Isaiah 22:14 says this iniquity shall not be atoned for until you die.
Asks what circumstances constitute desecration of God's name.
Rav: an important figure who buys meat on credit without paying at once; Abaye limits this to places where payment is not demanded later.
Ravina's city collects payment; Abaye paid each partner separately and later reckoned the balance.
R. Yohanan: a Torah scholar seen walking four cubits without Torah or phylacteries desecrates God's name.
Yitzhak of R. Yannai's school: when friends are embarrassed by one's reputation, that is desecration.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: people saying a master should forgive a student's sins is desecration.
Abaye introduces a baraita on loving God.
Deuteronomy 6:5, and you shall love the Lord, is read as making God's name beloved.
Ways to make God's name beloved: study, serve scholars, and deal pleasantly and honestly with people.
Good conduct gives people praise for the teacher and parents; bad conduct brings woe.
Isaiah 49:3, You are My servant Israel in whom I will be glorified, applies to the good scholar.
Scholar who lacks honest dealing and pleasant speech brings woe on himself, teacher, and parent.
Ezekiel 36:20: nations say of them, these are God's people yet they left His land, showing desecration.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina: great is repentance, for it brings healing to the world.
Hosea 14:5: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.
Rabbi Hama raises a contradiction between Jeremiah 3:14 and Jeremiah 3:22.
Resolved: the first refers to repentance from love, the second to repentance from fear.
Rabbi Yehuda raises a further contradiction between Jeremiah 3:22 and Jeremiah 3:14, about who can repent.
No contradiction: one case is repentance from love or fear, the other repentance through suffering.
Rabbi Levi: great is repentance, for it reaches the heavenly throne.
Hosea 14:2: Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, shows repentance reaches God.

ranges.en: R. Yohanan: repentance overrides even a Torah prohibition, such as returning to a divorced wife.
Jeremiah 3:1 compares Israel to a wife who returns to her husband after adultery, yet God invites return.
R. Yonatan: repentance hastens the redemption.
Isaiah 59:20: a redeemer comes to Zion for those who turn from transgression in Jacob.
Reish Lakish: intentional sins of a penitent are counted as unwitting ones.
Hosea 14:2: Return Israel, for you have stumbled in your iniquity, supports the teaching.
Asks: iniquity is intentional, so why does the verse call it stumbling?
Reish Lakish elsewhere says sins become merits, so the two teachings seem to contradict.
Resolved: one repents out of love, making sins merits; out of fear, sins count as unwitting.
R. Shmuel bar Nahmani citing R. Yonatan: repentance lengthens a person's life.
Ezekiel 18:27: the wicked who turns from his wickedness shall preserve his life.
Rabba bar Mari: unlike flesh and blood, one who sins privately can be appeased by words with God.
God is appeased by words when one repents for a private transgression.
Hosea 14:3: take with you words and return to God.
Repentance is considered a favor done for God.
Hosea 14:3, Accept that which is good, supports the favor point.
Repentance is credited as if one had sacrificed bulls.
Hosea 14:3: so we will render for bulls the offering of our lips.
Lest one say it is only like an obligatory bull, not a free-will offering.
Hosea 14:5 says repentance is like a free-will offering.
Baraita of R. Meir: repentance of one individual brings forgiveness to the whole world, based on Hosea 14:5.
Asks what circumstances show that one has fully repented.
Rav Yehuda: one faces the same sin with the same woman and resists, proving full repentance.
Rav raises a contradiction: Psalms 32:1 says the sin is hidden, Proverbs 28:13 says hiders do not prosper.
Resolved: a publicized sin should be publicly repented, an unpublicized one need not be.
Rav Nahman: public repentance is for sins against others, private repentance for sins against God.
Baraita of R. Yosei bar Yehuda: a person is forgiven the first three times but not the fourth.
Amos 2:6 for three transgressions but four, and Job 33:29 on God acting twice or three times.
Asks what the phrase and it says is adding.
Lest one say this applies to communities but not individuals.
Job 33:29 applies to an individual, with the fourth time not forgiven per Amos 2:6.
Tosefta: a sin confessed on one Yom Kippur need not be confessed again unless repeated.
Proverbs 26:11: a fool who repeats folly is like a dog returning to its vomit.
R. Eliezer ben Yaakov: confessing old sins in later years is even more praiseworthy.
Psalms 51:5: my sin is ever before me, showing remembered sins are humbling.
Asks how to read the dog returning to its vomit verse, given the praise of confession.
Rav Huna: a sin repeated becomes permitted to the person.
Asks: can it enter your mind that a repeated sin becomes permitted?
Rather, it becomes as if permitted, but the sin must still be detailed.
One must detail the sin in confession; Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava cites Exodus 32:31 as support.
R. Akiva's position on confession.
Psalms 32:1 that the forgiven sin is hidden, R. Akiva's support for not detailing.
Asks what Moses meant by saying they made a golden god.
R. Yannai: Moses said the people were given abundant silver and gold until they said enough, which caused the sin.
Moses asks that his disgrace be written explicitly.
Numbers 20:12: because you did not believe in Me, to sanctify Me.
David asks that his disgrace not be written.
Psalms 32:1: fortunate is he whose sin is hidden, supporting David.
Parable: two women flogged, one asks that her offense be publicized so she is not confused with the other.
One exposes hypocrites so people do not think their wickedness is righteous, because of desecration of God's name.
Ezekiel 3:20: when a righteous man turns from righteousness, I will place a stumbling block before him.
Full repentance suspends the decree of punishment, even when a sentence was already signed.
The tranquility of the wicked leads to ruin, and a judge leaves power as naked as he entered.
Rav's practice: before judging, he would say he goes to die voluntarily and returns empty-handed.
Rava's practice: before going to judge, he would say the same of himself.

ranges.en: Rav's practice continues: he goes out voluntarily, and when followed by a crowd he quotes Job against arrogance.
Job 20:6-7: even one whose head reaches the clouds perishes like dung, so power is not lasting.
Rav Zutra, carried on shoulders on Shabbat, recites Proverbs to avoid arrogance.
Proverbs 27:24 and 18:5: power is not forever, and it is not good to favor the wicked.
It was not good for Ahab to be honored in this world, so he lost his share in the World-to-Come.
I Kings 21:29 shows Ahab's punishment deferred; Proverbs 18:5 completes the verse for the righteous.
It was good for Moses not to be honored in this world.
Numbers 20:12, because you did not believe in Me, supports Moses's lack of honor.
Had Moses believed, his time to depart the world still would not have come.
The righteous merit for their children and descendants, as the surviving sons of Aaron were spared.
Leviticus 10:12: the remaining sons of Aaron show that their father's merit protected them.
The wicked bring liability on their descendants, as Canaan's children were kept as servants.
Whoever accumulates merit for the public avoids sin, while whoever causes the public to sin cannot repent.
Asks the reason that the meritorious man is protected from sin.
So that he is not in Gehenna while his students are in Eden.
Psalms 16:10: You will not abandon my soul to the nether-world, supporting the Eden reward.
Whoever causes the public to sin has almost no ability to repent.
So he is not in Eden while his students are in Gehenna.
Proverbs 28:17: a man laden with blood hastens to the pit, and none will support him.
Asks why the mishna says I will sin and I will repeat twice.
Rav Huna in Rav's name: a repeated sin is as if permitted, so the phrase repeats.
Mishna: Yom Kippur does not atone for one who says I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone.
Perhaps the mishna is not like Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, as a baraita states.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: Yom Kippur atones for all Torah sins, repented or not.
Even so, the mishna is different when sin is committed only because Yom Kippur will atone.
Rav Yosef bar Havu raises a contradiction: sins against people are not atoned, yet 1 Samuel 2:25 says the judge forgives.
1 Samuel 2:25, if a man sins against another God shall pray for him, supports forgiveness by prayer.
Rabbi Abbahu: Elohim there means a judge, so atonement occurs only after a court ruling.
Rav Yosef's retort: then the latter clause must also be read as judgment.
Rabbi Abbahu: the second clause refers to repentance and good deeds, so pll means forgiveness.
Rabbi Yitzhak: one who angers a friend, even verbally, must appease him.
Proverbs 6:1-3 on becoming a guarantor and humbling oneself before the neighbor.
Interpretation: pay the money owed, or else send many friends to ask forgiveness.
Rav Hisda: one must appease with three rows of three people.
Job 33:27 on coming before men, with three expressions of sin supporting three rows.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: one should not ask forgiveness from a friend more than three times.
Genesis 50:17 uses please three times, supporting the limit of three requests.
If the insulted one has died, bring ten people to his grave and confess before them.
Story: Rabbi Yirmeya insulted Rabbi Abba and sat at his threshold, and Rabbi Abba came out to appease him.
Story: Rabbi Zeira paced before a person who had insulted him so that he could come and appease him.
Story: Rav planned to appease a butcher on Yom Kippur eve, but a bone from the butcher's splitting killed the butcher.
Rav was reciting the Torah portion before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
