ranges.en: Narrative: Rav repeatedly rereads for arriving scholars, which offends Rabbi Ḥanina, and Rav fails to win his forgiveness for years.
Why would Rav act this way, given the rule about asking forgiveness?
Objection: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina taught that one should not ask forgiveness more than three times.
Rav was different because he was exceptionally pious and went beyond the letter of the law.
Then how could Rabbi Ḥanina refuse forgiveness after repeated requests?
Objection: Rava taught that one who suppresses his anger is forgiven all his sins.
Rabbi Ḥanina dreamed Rav was hanged on a palm tree, a sign he would head a yeshiva, so he delayed forgiveness to send Rav to Babylonia.
A baraita says confession is required at evening, and optionally again at each later prayer, including after eating and at ne'ila.
Where in the Yom Kippur prayers is the confession recited?
An individual confesses after his Amida, while the prayer leader confesses in the middle of the Amida.
What exactly is the wording of the confession?
Rav, Shmuel and Levi each offer a different opening phrase for the confession.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the confession opens with Master of the Universe.
Rabbi Yehuda gives a confession text about iniquities being too many to count.
Rav Hamnuna's confession text states human unworthiness and asks to be forgiven without suffering.
The Gemara notes which confession Rava and Rav Hamnuna Zuta used on Yom Kippur.
Mar Zutra rules that saying the words but we have sinned suffices, making the rest of the confession unnecessary.
Bar Hamdudei's account of Shmuel standing at the words but we have sinned supports the view that this is the core of confession.
A mishna in Ta'anit lists the times priests bless the people and the occasions of the closing of the gates, including Yom Kippur.
What is the closing of the gates, the ne'ila prayer?
Rav holds that ne'ila is an additional Amida prayer.
Shmuel holds that ne'ila is only a confession beginning with what are we and what are our lives.
Objection from a baraita: on Yom Kippur one prays seven blessings and confesses at every prayer, including ne'ila, which supports Rav.
This baraita is a tannaitic dispute, so it does not settle the question against Shmuel.
A baraita says the evening prayer on Yom Kippur ends with confession according to Rabbi Meir, and the Rabbis let one choose.
The baraita refutes Shmuel, since all agree that ne'ila is a complete prayer.
Ulla bar Rav led ne'ila before Rava, opening with You chose us and ending with what are we, and Rava praised him.
Rav Huna son of Rav Natan says an individual recites this confession after his own Amida prayer.
Rav says the ne'ila prayer exempts one from the evening prayer.
Gemara explains Rav's reasoning: since ne'ila is an additional prayer, once he has prayed it, no further evening prayer is needed.
Did Rav really say this, given his ruling that the halakha follows the view that evening prayer is optional?
Objection: Rav ruled that evening prayer is optional, so exemption makes no sense under that view.
Rav spoke according to the view that evening prayer is mandatory, which ne'ila can still fulfill.
Objection from a baraita on evening prayers after Yom Kippur and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel's custom of praying the full eighteen blessings.

ranges.en: Explains that the matter is a tannaitic dispute, tied to whether havdala is recited in the Ḥonen HaDa'at blessing.
A baraita says that all who need immersion immerse in their usual way on Yom Kippur, and a man with a seminal emission may immerse until afternoon prayer.
Rabbi Yosei holds that the seminal-emission immersion is permitted for the whole day.
Objection: a parallel baraita has Rabbi Yosei forbid immersion from the afternoon prayer onward, contradicting the previous baraita.
Not a real contradiction: one statement concerns a man who already prayed ne'ila, the other one who has not.
If he already prayed ne'ila, what is the Rabbis' reason to permit immersion, since it seems pointless?
The Rabbis hold that immersion at its proper time is a mitzva even when it is not needed for prayer.
By inference, Rabbi Yosei must hold that proper-time immersion is not a mitzva.
Objection from a baraita about divine name written on flesh: Rabbi Yosei lets one immerse normally, which seems to conflict with that inference.
The disputes concern proper-time immersion, and the Rabbi Yosei of that baraita is Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, resolving the conflict.
A baraita says one who sees seminal emission on Yom Kippur immerses, and rubs his skin in the evening.
Why rub in the evening, since the immersion has already happened and the matter is past?
Instead, the rubbing should be done from the evening before Yom Kippur, in case immersion becomes necessary.
A tanna taught before Rav Naḥman that one who sees seminal emission on Yom Kippur has his sins forgiven.
Objection: a baraita says such sins are arranged, not forgiven, which seems to contradict the statement.
Arranged means they are set in order to be forgiven, so the two teachings agree.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that one who sees seminal emission should worry all year, but if he survives, he is assured of the World-to-Come.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak supports this with the image of a satiated man while the world is hungry.
Rav Dimi reports from Eretz Yisrael that seminal emission on Yom Kippur signals a long life with offspring, citing Isaiah 53:10.
Closing formula marking the end of the tractate Yoma and the completion of the chapter.
